title: Arakhin 19
description: Why an elderly woman keeps a third of her valuation and an elderly man does not, the close of chapter four, and the opening of chapter five: vowing one’s weight, one’s height or the weight of a limb, what yad and regel mean in the Torah and in vows, and how the court assesses one who vows the value of his hand.
topics: 👵 “An elderly man in the home is a burden; an elderly woman, a treasure”
📖 Hadran: chapter 4, HaSeg Yad, ends; chapter 5, HaOmer Mishkali Alai, begins
⚖️ “My weight is upon me”: silver, gold, pitch, onions, and the mother of Yirmatya
📏 “My height” and “my full height”: a stiff rod or a bendable one, and Rabbi Akiva’s superfluous language
🪣 Weighing a forearm in a barrel of water and donkey flesh: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
✋ Yad and regel: in the Torah, in the Temple, for tefillin, for the Festivals, for ḥalitza and in vows
💰 “The value of my hand”: Rava’s assessment of damages and Abaye’s slave with one hand written to his first master
❓ Rava’s chain of dilemmas: assessed by three or by ten, and vowing one’s assessment twice

a2.he: וּמַאי שְׁנָא נְקֵבָה, דְּכִי מִיזַּקְנָא קָיְימָא אַתִּילְּתָא, וּמַאי שְׁנָא זָכָר דְּלָא קָאֵי אַתִּילְּתָא? אָמַר חִזְקִיָּה: אָמְרִי אִינָשֵׁי: סָבָא בְּבֵיתָא — פָּאחָא בְּבֵיתָא, סָבְתָא בְּבֵיתָא — סִימָא בְּבֵיתָא.

a4.he: מַתְנִי׳ הָאוֹמֵר: ״מְשַׁקְּלִי עָלַי״ נוֹתֵן מִשְׁקָלוֹ, אִם כֶּסֶף כָּסֶף, וְאִם זָהָב זָהָב. מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאַמָּה שֶׁל יַרְמַטְיָא שֶׁאָמְרָה: ״מִשְׁקַל בִּתִּי עָלַי״, וְעָלְתָה לִירוּשָׁלַיִם וְשַׁקְלַהּ מִשְׁקָלָהּ זָהָב.

a5.he: ״מִשְׁקַל יְדֵי עָלַי״, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: מְמַלֵּא חָבִית מַיִם, וּמַכְנִיסָהּ עַד מַרְפֵּיקוֹ, וְשׁוֹקֵל מִבְּשַׂר חֲמוֹר וַעֲצָמוֹת וְגִידִים וְנוֹתֵן לְתוֹכָהּ עַד שֶׁתִּתְמַלֵּא. אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: וְכִי הֵיאַךְ אֶפְשָׁר לְכַוֵּין בָּשָׂר כְּנֶגֶד בָּשָׂר וַעֲצָמוֹת כְּנֶגֶד עֲצָמוֹת? אֶלָּא שָׁמִין אֶת הַיָּד כַּמָּה הִיא רְאוּיָה לִשְׁקוֹל.

a6.he: גְּמָ׳ מַאי ״אִם כֶּסֶף כֶּסֶף אִם זָהָב זָהָב״? אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: פֵּירַשׁ כֶּסֶף — כֶּסֶף, פֵּירַשׁ זָהָב — זָהָב. פְּשִׁיטָא! הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן: טַעְמָא דְּפֵירַשׁ, הָא לֹא פֵּירֵשׁ — פָּטַר נַפְשֵׁיהּ בְּכֹל דְּהוּ.

a7.he: כִּרְחָבָה, דְּאָמַר רַחֲבָה: בְּאַתְרָא דְּתִקְלֵי כּוֹפְרָא — פָּטַר נַפְשֵׁיהּ אֲפִילּוּ בַּכּוֹפְרָא. פְּשִׁיטָא! לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאִיכָּא דִּתְקֵל וְאִיכָּא דְּכָיֵיל. מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: כֵּיוָן דְּכוּלְּהוּ לָא תִּקְלֵי — לָא, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.

a8.he: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: בְּאַתְרָא דְּתִקְלֵי שַׁמְכֵי, פָּטַר נַפְשֵׁיהּ אֲפִילּוּ בְּשַׁמְכֵי. פְּשִׁיטָא! לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּבָתַר דְּשָׁקְלִי שָׁדוּ תְּרֵי תְּלָתָא. מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: בְּטִיל תּוֹרַת מִשְׁקַל, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.

a9.he: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאַמָּה שֶׁל יַרְמַטְיָא וְכוּ׳. מַעֲשֶׂה לִסְתּוֹר?!

a10.he: חַסּוֹרֵי מְחַסְּרָא וְהָכִי קָתָנֵי, וְאִם אָדָם חָשׁוּב הוּא, אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא פָּרֵישׁ — לְפִי כְּבוֹדוֹ אָמְרִינַן, וּמַעֲשֶׂה בְּאַמָּה שֶׁל יַרְמַטְיָא שֶׁאָמְרָה ״מִשְׁקַל בִּתִּי עָלַי״, וְעָלְתָה לִירוּשָׁלַיִם וְשַׁקְלוּהּ וְנָתְנָה מִשְׁקָלָהּ זָהָב.

a11.he: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: הָאוֹמֵר ״קוֹמָתִי עָלַי״ נוֹתֵן שַׁרְבִיט שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִכְפָּף, ״מָלֵא קוֹמָתִי עָלַי״ נוֹתֵן שַׁרְבִיט הַנִּכְפָּף. מֵיתִיבִי: ״קוֹמָתִי עָלַי״, ״מָלֵא קוֹמָתִי עָלַי״ — נוֹתֵן שַׁרְבִיט שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִכְפָּף.

a12.he: הוּא דְּאָמַר כְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, דְּדָיֵיק לִישָּׁנָא יַתִּירָא, דִּתְנַן: לֹא אֶת הַבּוֹר וְלֹא הַדּוּת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכָּתַב עוֹמְקָהּ וְרוּמַהּ, וְצָרִיךְ לִיקַּח לוֹ דֶּרֶךְ, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא.

a13.he: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ, וּמוֹדֶה רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא בִּזְמַן שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ״חוּץ מֵאֵלּוּ״ שֶׁאֵין צָרִיךְ לִיקַּח לוֹ דֶּרֶךְ. אַלְמָא, כֵּיוָן דְּלָא צְרִיךְ וְקָאָמַר — לְטַפּוֹיֵי מִילְּתָא קָאָתֵי, הָכָא נָמֵי, כֵּיוָן דְּלָא צְרִיךְ וְקָאָמַר — לְטַפּוֹיֵי מִילְּתָא קָאָתֵי.

b2.he: מִשְׁקַל יָדִי עָלַי וְכוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״מִשְׁקָל יְדֵי״ וּ״מִשְׁקַל רַגְלֵי עָלַי״, רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: מֵבִיא חָבִית וּמְמַלֵּא מַיִם, וּמַכְנִיס בְּיַד עַד הָאַצִּיל, וּבָרֶגֶל עַד הָאַרְכּוּבָּה.

b3.he: וְשׁוֹקֵל בְּשַׂר חֲמוֹר גִּידִים וַעֲצָמוֹת, וְנוֹתֵן לְתוֹכָהּ עַד שֶׁתִּתְמַלֵּא, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לְדָבָר, זֵכֶר לַדָּבָר, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״אֲשֶׁר בְּשַׂר חֲמוֹרִים בְּשָׂרָם״.

b4.he: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: הֵיאַךְ אֶפְשָׁר לְכַוֵּין בָּשָׂר כְּנֶגֶד בְּשַׂר, גִּידִים כְּנֶגֶד גִּידִים, עֲצָמוֹת כְּנֶגֶד עֲצָמוֹת? אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: אוֹמְדִין. אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: עַד שֶׁאוֹמְדִין, יָמוֹדּוּ אֶת הַיָּד. וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה: כַּמָּה דְּאֶפְשָׁר עָבְדִינַן.

b5.he: בַּיָּד עַד הָאַצִּיל, וּרְמִינְהוּ: קִידּוּשׁ יָדַיִם וְרַגְלַיִם בְּמִקְדָּשׁ עַד הַפֶּרֶק.

b6.he: דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא עַד הַפֶּרֶק, בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם, וּדְאוֹרָיְיתָא עַד הַפֶּרֶק? וְהָא גַּבֵּי תְּפִילִּין דִּכְתִיב ״יָדְךָ״, וְתַנָּא דְבֵי מְנַשֶּׁה: ״יָדְךָ״ — זוֹ קִיבּוֹרִית!

b7.he: דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא — קִיבּוּרִית כּוּלַּהּ, בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם, וְקִידּוּשׁ יָדַיִם וְרַגְלַיִם בַּמִּקְדָּשׁ — הִילְכְתָא גְּמִירִי לַהּ.

b8.he: בָּרֶגֶל עַד הָאַרְכּוּבָּה, וּרְמִינְהוּ: ״רְגָלִים״ — פְּרָט לְבַעֲלֵי קַבִּין!

b9.he: בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם, וּדְאוֹרָיְיתָא — פְּרָט לְבַעֲלֵי קַבִּין?

b10.he: וְהָא גַּבֵּי חֲלִיצָה, דִּכְתִיב: ״רַגְלוֹ״, וְתָנָא: חָלְצָה מִן הָאַרְכּוּבָּה וּלְמַטָּה — חֲלִיצָתָהּ כְּשֵׁרָה!

b11.he: שָׁאנֵי הָתָם, דְּאָמַר קְרָא: ״מֵעַל רַגְלוֹ״. אִי הָכִי, לְמַעְלָה מֵהָאַרְכּוּבָּה נָמֵי? ״מָעַל״, וְלֹא מָעַל דְּמֵעַל.

b12.he: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ, הַאי אִיסְתְּוֵירָא עַד אַרְעָא נָחֵית, דְּאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ מִיפְסָק פְּסֵיק, הֲוָה לֵיהּ אִיסְתְּוֵירָא ״מֵעַל״, וְשָׁקָא ״מֵעַל״ דְּ״מֵעַל״. רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא מִיפְסָק פְּסֵיק, כֹּל דְּבַהֲדֵי כַּרְעָא כְּכַרְעָא דָּמֵי.

b13.he: מַתְנִי׳ ״דָּמֵי יְדֵי עָלַי״ — שָׁמִין אוֹתוֹ כַּמָּה הוּא שָׁוָה בַּיָּד וּבְלֹא יָד. זֶה חוֹמֶר בַּנְּדָרִים מִבַּעֲרָכִין.

b14.he: גְּמָ׳ הֵיכִי שָׁיְימִינַן לֵיהּ? אָמַר רָבָא: אוֹמְדִין אוֹתוֹ אוֹמֶד שֶׁל נִזָּקִין.

b15.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: מִי דָּמֵי? הָתָם גַּבְרָא זִילָא הוּא, הָכָא גַּבְרָא שְׁבִיחַ הוּא.

b16.he: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: אוֹמְדִין כַּמָּה אָדָם רוֹצֶה לִיתֵּן בְּעֶבֶד הָעוֹשֶׂה מְלָאכָה בְּיָדוֹ אַחַת לָעוֹשֶׂה בִּשְׁתֵּי יָדָיו. יָדוֹ אַחַת מַאי נִיהוּ, וְאִידַּךְ פְּסִיקָא? הַיְינוּ הָךְ! אֶלָּא, יָדוֹ מוּכְתֶּבֶת לְרַבּוֹ רִאשׁוֹן.

b17.he: בָּעֵי רָבָא: אֲמָדוּהוּ אוֹמֶד שֶׁל נִזָּקִין, וְאָמַר ״דְּמֵי עָלַי״, מַהוּ? מִי אָמַר: הָא אֲמָדוּהוּ חֲדָא זִימְנָא, אוֹ דִילְמָא שָׁאנֵי אוּמְדָּנָא דְּבֵי עַשְׂרָה מֵאוּמְדָּנָא דְּבֵי תְלָתָא?

b18.he: אִם תִּמְצָא לוֹמַר: שָׁאנֵי אוּמְדָּנָא דְּבֵי עֲשָׂרָה מֵאוּמְדָּנָא דְּבֵי תְּלָתָא, אָמַר: ״דְּמֵי עָלַי״ וַאֲמָדוּהוּ, וְחָזַר וְאָמַר: ״דְּמֵי עָלַי״, מַהוּ? הָכָא וַדַּאי אֲמָדוּהוּ בֵּי עֲשָׂרָה, אוֹ דִילְמָא שָׁבַח בֵּינֵי וּבֵינֵי?

b19.he: אָמַר: ״דְּמֵי עָלַי״, וְלֹא אֲמָדוּהוּ, וְחָזַר וְאָמַר: ״דְּמֵי עָלַי״, מַהוּ? הָכָא וַדַּאי

messages.text: Continued from 18b: a baraita listed periods counted in full years, among them those stated “with regard to a son and with regard to a daughter.” Rav said this refers to valuations; Rav Yosef said it refers to the chapter Yotze Dofen in tractate Nidda. Rav Yosef argues that if the baraita meant valuations, the wording “a son … a daughter” would be unsuitable:

Rather, the baraita should have stated: With regard to the male and with regard to the female, which are the terms the Torah uses with regard to valuations. The terms son and daughter are used in Yotze Dofen.

notes.he: כלישנא דקרא דכתיב בערכין (ויקרא כז) אם זכר אם נקבה ולא כתיב בן ובת אבל יוצא דופן כוליה בן ובת תנינן:
notes.en: It should have said “with regard to the male and with regard to the female”: in the language of the verse, as it is written about valuations (Leviticus 27), “if male … if female,” and “son” and “daughter” are not written. But the whole of [the chapter] Yotze Dofen we learned in terms of son and daughter.

notes.he: כדכתיב באורייתא והיה [ערכך] הזכר ואם נקבה היא אלא ש"מ לפירקא דיוצא דופן קא מיירי:
notes.en: It should have said “with regard to the male and with regard to the female”: as it is written in the Torah, “then your valuation shall be for the male … and if it be a female.” Rather, conclude from it that it is speaking of the chapter Yotze Dofen.

messages.text: With regard to valuations: And what is different with regard to a female, that when she ages past sixty years she stands at a valuation of ten shekels, one-third of her previous valuation of thirty shekels, and what is different with regard to a male, that when he ages past sixty, at which point he has a valuation of fifteen shekels, he does not stand at even one-third of his previous valuation of fifty shekels?

notes.he: בערכין דנקבה כי מזקנא יותר על ששים קיימא אתילתא דערך ילדה שלשים שקל וערך זקנה עשרת שקלים:
notes.en: And what is different: in valuations, that a female, when she ages beyond sixty, stands at one-third, for the valuation of a young woman is thirty shekels and the valuation of an old woman ten shekels.

notes.he: דכי עבר על ששים לא קאי אתילתא דבציר ערך זקן טפי מתילתא בערך ילד דילד חמשים שקלים וזקן ט"ו שקלים:
notes.en: And what is different about a male: that when he passes sixty he does not stand at one-third, for the valuation of an old man is less than one-third of the valuation of a young man: a young man is fifty shekels and an old man fifteen shekels.

notes.he: דכתיב מבן עשרים שנה עד בן ששים שנה ואם נקבה היא והיה ערכך שלשים שקל וכתיב בבת ס' שנה ומעלה לנקבה עשרת שקלים דהיינו תילתא:
notes.en: She stands at one-third: as it is written, “from twenty years old until sixty years old … and if it be a female, then your valuation shall be thirty shekels,” and it is written of sixty years and up, “for the female ten shekels,” which is one-third.

notes.he: דכתיב מבן עשרים שנה עד בן ששים חמשים שקל ואילו בבן ששים שנה ומעלה כתיב חמשה עשר שקל דהיינו בציר מתילתא]:
notes.en: The male does not stand at one-third: as it is written, from twenty years old until sixty, fifty shekels, whereas of sixty years and up it is written fifteen shekels, which is less than one-third.

messages.text: people say a popular saying: If there is an elderly man in the home, there is a burden [paḥa] in the home, as he does not help with anything; if there is an elderly woman in the home, there is a treasure in the home, as she assists with various domestic labors.

notes.he: שבר שאינו אלא למשא. ל"א פחחא גרסינן לשון ערום ועריה דמתרגמינן לערום פחיח בתרגום של נביאים (יחזקאל טז):
notes.en: Paḥa: a broken thing that is good only as a load. Another version: we read paḥḥa, a term for naked and bare, as the Aramaic translation of the Prophets renders “naked” as paḥiaḥ (Ezekiel 16).

notes.he: מטמון שיכולה לטרוח ולעשות מלאכה בזקנותה:
notes.en: Sima: a hidden treasure, for she can exert herself and do work in her old age.

notes.he: מוקש:
notes.en: A paḥa in the house: a snare.

notes.he: מטמון שמשמרת כל מה שיש בבית:
notes.en: A sima in the house: a treasure, who guards everything in the house.

notes.he: הדרן עלך השג יד
notes.en: Hadran alakh HaSeg Yad: we will return to you, chapter “Affordability.”

messages.text: הדרן עלך השג יד · Hadran alakh HaSeg Yad: we will return to you, chapter 4, “Affordability.”
Chapter 5 · האומר משקלי עלי · HaOmer Mishkali Alai: pledging one’s weight, one’s height, the value of a limb, or one’s “head” to the Temple.
Mishna
One who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate my weight, gives his weight to the Temple treasury; if he specified silver he donates silver, and if he specified gold he donates gold.

notes.he: מתני' האומר משקלי עלי:
notes.en: Mishna: One who says: My weight is upon me. [A heading only.]

notes.he: מתני' האומר משקלי עלי:
notes.en: Mishna: One who says: My weight is upon me. [A heading only.]

notes.he: לתת להקדש:
notes.en: One who says: My weight is upon me: to give to the Temple treasury.

notes.he: נדר נותן כסף משקלו:
notes.en: If silver: if he vowed silver, he gives his weight in silver.

messages.text: There was an incident involving the mother of Yirmatya, who said: It is incumbent upon me to donate the weight of my daughter, and she ascended to Jerusalem and paid her daughter’s weight in gold to the Temple treasury.

notes.he: שם האשה:
notes.en: Yirmatya: the name of the woman.

messages.text: In the case of one who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate the weight of my forearm, how does he ascertain the weight of his forearm?

notes.he: היאך הוא שוקל אם רוצה מכביד ואם רוצה מיקל:
notes.en: The weight of my forearm is upon me: how can he weigh it? If he wishes, he presses down and makes it heavy, and if he wishes, he lightens it.

messages.text: He fills a barrel with water and inserts his arm up to his elbow into the water. And in order to measure the displacement, he weighs donkey flesh, and bones, and sinews and places it into the barrel until it fills, and the water level reaches the top of the barrel. He then donates the weight of the meat and the bones to the Temple treasury.

notes.he: לתוכו:
notes.en: He fills a barrel with water and inserts it: into it.

notes.he: אציל שקורין איישיל"א וכשמכניסה יוצאין המים וכשמוציאה נמצאת חסירה:
notes.en: Up to his marpek: the atzil, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). When he inserts it the water spills out, and when he takes it out the barrel is found lacking.

notes.he: שמשקל בשר חמור כמשקל בשר אדם ויהיו באותו בשר גידין ועצמות לפי מה שיש ביד לפי שאין משקל עצמות וגידים שוה למשקל בשר ונותן לתוכה עד שתתמלא דהשתא איכא נפח כשיעור ידו וכפי אותו משקל יתן:
notes.en: And he weighs donkey flesh: for the weight of donkey flesh is like the weight of human flesh. And in that flesh there should be sinews and bones in proportion to what is in the arm, since the weight of bones and sinews is not the same as the weight of flesh. And places it into it until it fills: for now there is a volume the size of his arm, and according to that weight he gives.

notes.he: פי' רש"י אציל שקורין אשייל"א בלע"ז ולא נראה שהרי בברייתא בגמרא תני עד האציל ואי אפשר שהוא אשייל"א דאיתא בפרק ב' דזבחים (דף יח:) ולא יחגרו ביזע שלא היו חוגרים במקום זיעה לא למטה ממתניהם ולא למעלה מאציליהם (ולא תחת אצילי) [אלא כנגד אצילי] ידיהם ואי אמרת דהוא אשייל"א אדרבה שם הוא מקום זיעה לכך פירש ר"י דהוא שקורין קוד"א ובמנחות (דף לז. ושם) ובזבחים (דף יט.) הארכתי:
notes.en: Up to his marpek: Rashi explained, the atzil, which is called (an Old French gloss) in the vernacular. This does not seem right, for in the baraita in the Gemara it teaches “up to the atzil,” and it cannot be [what Rashi’s gloss names], for it is stated in the second chapter of Zevaḥim (18b): “They shall not gird themselves with what causes sweat” [Ezekiel 44:18], meaning that they would not gird themselves at a place of sweat, neither below their loins nor above their atzilim, but opposite the atzilim of their arms. And if you say it is [what Rashi’s gloss names], on the contrary, that is a place of sweat. Therefore Ri explained that it is what is called (an Old French gloss) [that is, the elbow, as the Davidson English renders it]. I have discussed this at length in Menaḥot (37a) and in Zevaḥim (19a).

notes.he: עד בית שחיו שהוא הכתף וכמה שמכניס ידו לחבית יוצאין המים:
notes.en: Up to his marpek: up to his armpit, which is the shoulder; and as much as he inserts his arm into the barrel, that much water spills out.

notes.he: ונוטל בשר חמור וגידים ועצמות כנגד היד ונותן לחבית עד שתתמלא שיגביהו המים עד למעלה ואח"כ יוציא [בשר חמור לחוץ היינו משקל ידו] ולפי אותו המשקל יתן:
notes.en: And he weighs: he takes donkey flesh, sinews and bones corresponding to the arm and puts them into the barrel until it fills, so that the water rises to the top. Afterward he takes the donkey flesh out; that is the weight of his arm, and according to that weight he gives.

messages.text: Displacement is according to volume, not according to weight; and how then is it possible to match the amount of the donkey flesh with the flesh of a person and the volume of the donkey’s bones with his bones? Rather, the court appraises how much the forearm is likely to weigh.

notes.dh: וכי היאך אפשר לכווין [בשר כנגד בשר]
notes.he: ליתן בשר חמור כנגד בשר ועצמות כנגד עצם שבזרוע. שמא זרוע העצם יותר מזה העצם ושוקל יותר:
notes.en: And how is it possible to match flesh with flesh: to put donkey flesh against the flesh and bones against the bone of the arm? Perhaps the bone of the arm is larger than this bone, and it weighs more.

notes.he: אומדין את היד כמה היא ראויה לשקול בלא משקל:
notes.en: Rather, they appraise the arm: they estimate how much it is likely to weigh, without a weight.

messages.text: Gemara
What is the meaning of the mishna’s statement: If silver, silver, and if gold, gold?
messages.quote: if he specified silver he donates silver, and if he specified gold he donates gold

messages.text: If one specified that he vows to donate his weight in silver he donates silver, and if he specified gold he donates gold.
Isn’t that obvious?

This is what the mishna is teaching us: The reason he donates silver or gold is that he specified silver or gold, from which it may be inferred that if he did not specify the means of payment, he may exempt himself with any material.

notes.he: כל מה שהוא רוצה לשקול ישקול:
notes.en: Gemara. [He may exempt] himself with anything: whatever he wishes to weigh, he weighs.

notes.he: כלומר באיזה דבר שירצה שרגילין בני אדם לשוקלו:
notes.en: Even with anything: that is, with whatever he wishes that people usually sell by weight.

messages.text: And this is in accordance with a statement of Raḥava,
In a place where merchants weigh pitch when selling it, one who vows his weight may exempt himself by donating his weight even in pitch.

notes.he: זפת:
notes.en: With kofra: pitch.

notes.he: שמוכרים זפת במשקל:
notes.en: In a place where they weigh kofra: where they sell pitch by weight.

notes.he: זפת]:
notes.en: Kofra: pitch.

messages.text: Isn’t that obvious?

No, the statement of Raḥava is necessary in a place where there are merchants who weigh pitch and there are others who measure its volume. Lest you say: Since not all merchants weigh pitch one may not fulfill his vow by donating his weight in pitch, Raḥava teaches us that as there are merchants there who sell pitch by weight, one can fulfill his vow in that manner.

notes.he: מודד:
notes.en: Who measure: who sell by measure.

messages.text: In a place where merchants weigh onions when selling them, one who vowed his weight may exempt himself by donating his weight even in onions.

notes.he: בצלים:
notes.en: Shamkhei: onions.

notes.he: בצלים]:
notes.en: Shamkhei: onions.

messages.text: Again: isn’t that obvious?

No, the statement of Rav Pappa is necessary in a place where after they weigh the onions the merchants throw in two or three extra onions to the buyer. Lest you say that its status as a place where onions are sold by weight is void due to the additional onions, Rav Pappa teaches us that it is still considered a place where onions are sold by weight.

notes.he: כדרך המוכרין:
notes.en: They throw in two or three: as sellers do.

notes.he: ונמצא שאין נמכרין במשקל:
notes.en: Its status as weighed is void: and it turns out that they are not sold by weight.

notes.he: וא"ת בכל מקום נמי היו מעריכין יותר מן המשקל כדמוכח בבבא בתרא פרק המוכר את הספינה (בבא בתרא דף פח:)) והיכי ס"ד דבטלה תורת משקל וי"ל דהכי פירוש דהכא באתרא דשקלי שדו תרי תילתי יותר מן הכרע הלכך סלקא דעתך דבטלה כיון שנותן יותר מכדין:
notes.en: After they weigh they throw in two or three: And if you ask: everywhere, too, they would give more than the weight, as is evident in Bava Batra, chapter HaMokher et HaSefina (88b); so how could one have thought that the status of weight is void? One may answer that this is the meaning: here it is a place where they weigh and then throw in two or three beyond the [customary] tipping of the scale; therefore one might have thought that it is void, since he gives more than is due.

notes.he: לויתור לגירומין:
notes.en: They throw in two or three: as an extra, as a bonus.

notes.he: דלא בטיל ופטר נפשיה בהו:
notes.en: It teaches us: that it is not void, and he exempts himself with them.

messages.text: She said: It is incumbent upon me to donate the weight of my daughter, without specifying silver or gold, and she ascended to Jerusalem and paid her daughter’s weight in gold to the Temple treasury. Was an incident cited to contradict the previous ruling of the mishna? The mishna had stated: If silver, silver, and if gold, gold, which indicates that if one did not specify the means of payment he may exempt himself with any material that merchants sell by weight, whereas it can be inferred from the incident that one must pay the weight in gold.
messages.quote: an incident involving the mother of Yirmatya

notes.he: קתני רישא אם כסף כסף כו' ואוקימנא דקאתא לאשמועינן דאי לא פריש פטר נפשיה בכל דהו והדר תני באמה של ירמטיא שאמרה משקל בתי סתם עלי ושקלתה בזהב:
notes.en: An incident to contradict?: The first clause teaches “if silver, silver,” and so on, and we established that it comes to teach that if he did not specify, he may exempt himself with anything; and then it teaches about the mother of Yirmatya, who said “the weight of my daughter is upon me” without specifying, and she weighed her in gold.

notes.he: רישא אמרת הא משקלי עלי סתם פטר נפשיה בכל דהוא והשתא אמרת דנתנה משקלה זהב:
notes.en: An incident to contradict? In the first clause you said that with “my weight is upon me,” unspecified, he exempts himself with anything, and now you say that she gave her weight in gold.

messages.text: The mishna is incomplete and this is what it is teaching:

And if the one who vowed is a distinguished person, even though he did not specify silver or gold we say he must fulfill his vow in keeping with his socioeconomic status. And likewise, there was an incident involving the mother of Yirmatya, a very wealthy woman, who said: It is incumbent upon me to donate the weight of my daughter, and she ascended to Jerusalem and gave her daughter’s weight in gold to the Temple treasury.

notes.dh: כי אמרה סתם לפי כבודו (אמרינן) [אמדינן] ליה
notes.he: אם הוא עשיר (אמרינן) [אמדינן] ליה לחמור שבמשקלות:
notes.en: When she said it without specifying, we assess [the printed text reads “we say”] according to his dignity: if he is wealthy, we assess him by the most precious of the things that are weighed.

messages.text: One who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate my height, gives a thick rod that cannot be bent equivalent to his height. One who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate my full height, may give even a thin rod that can be bent, provided it is equivalent to his height.

notes.he: משמע כקומתו ונותן שרביט עב שלא יוכל לכופפו אם פירש כסף כסף ואם זהב זהב:
notes.en: My height: implies like his height, and he gives a thick rod, so thick that he cannot bend it; if he specified silver, silver, and if gold, gold.

notes.he: לא נתכוין אלא למדת גובה קומתו ולא לעובי:
notes.en: My full height: he intended only the measure of the height of his stature, and not its thickness.

notes.he: כלומר לתת שיעור קומתי של כסף או של זהב להקדש:
notes.en: My height is upon me: that is, to give the measure of my height in silver or in gold to the Temple treasury.

notes.he: של כסף עב שאינו נכפף מעצמו הואיל ואמר קומתו כלומר דבר שיכול לקיים מעצמו שאינו נכפף:
notes.en: He gives a rod: of silver, thick, that does not bend by itself, since he said “his height,” meaning something that can stand by itself and does not bend.

notes.he: כלומר כיון דאמר מלא קומתי בלבד שיהא ארוך כמותי קאמר אפי' דקה:
notes.en: My full height is upon me, he gives a rod that bends: that is, since he said “my full height,” he means only that it be as long as I am, even if it is thin.

messages.text: With regard to one who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate my height, or: It is incumbent upon me to donate my full height, he gives a thick rod that cannot be bent and that is equivalent to his height.
messages.lead: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita:

messages.text: Rav Yehuda says his statement in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that one can draw an inference from superfluous language.
messages.quote: my full height, may give even a thin rod that can be bent

notes.he: רב יהודה דאמר כר' עקיבא:
notes.en: Rav Yehuda states it in accordance with Rabbi Akiva. [A heading only.]

notes.he: תימה ברייתא מאן תניה לא רבי עקיבא ולא רבנן דעד כאן לא פליגי אלא דמ"ס מוכר בעין יפה מוכר ומר סבר מוכר בעין רעה מוכר ושייר הדרך לעצמו ואינו צריך לרבנן היתור לשון אבל היכא שהיתור צריך לעולם מודו רבנן דמהני וא"כ ברייתא כמאן תרמייה:
notes.en: He states it in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, and so on: It is puzzling: who taught the baraita? Neither Rabbi Akiva nor the Rabbis! For they disagree only in that one master holds that a seller sells generously and the other master holds that a seller sells grudgingly and reserves the path for himself; so according to the Rabbis the superfluous language [“except these”] is not needed. But where the superfluous language is needed, the Rabbis too would surely agree that it is effective. If so, whose view is the baraita?

notes.he: רב יהודה:
notes.en: He states it in accordance with Rabbi Akiva: Rav Yehuda does.

messages.text: If one sold his house without specification, he has sold neither the pit nor the cistern [dut] with it, even if he wrote in the document of sale: With its depth and its height. This is because anything that is ancillary to the house, e.g., pits and cisterns, must be mentioned explicitly in the contract. And the seller must purchase for himself a path through to the pit or cistern that he kept back, as he sold his rights to the area surrounding the house along with the house, and therefore he may no longer walk through that area. This is the statement of Rabbi Akiva.

notes.he: המוכר את הבית לא מכר את הבור שבה או את הדות. בור בחפירה בלא בנין כתלים ודות בבנין:
notes.en: Neither the pit: one who sells a house has not sold the pit in it, or the cistern. A bor is dug out without built walls, and a dut is built.

notes.he: מוכר ליקח לו דרך מן הלוקח לילך בה לאותו בור ודות שהרי כל הקרקע מכר לו ולא שייר דסבירא ליה מוכר בעין יפה מוכר:
notes.en: And he must: the seller must buy himself a path from the buyer, to walk through it to that pit and cistern, for he sold him all the land and reserved nothing; since he holds that a seller sells generously.

notes.dh: לא את הבור ולא את הדות
notes.he: לענין מכירה תנן בבבא בתרא. לא מכר לא את הבור ולא את הדות] אע"פ שכתב לו עומקה ורומה. של חצר ויש לומר שהללו בעומקה הן:
notes.en: Neither the pit nor the cistern: we learned this about sales in Bava Batra: he has sold neither the pit nor the cistern even though he wrote for him “its depth and its height” of the courtyard; and one might have said that these are part of its depth.

notes.he: מוכר מלוקח שילך בה לבורו דמוכר בעין יפה מוכר ולא שייר לעצמו דרך:
notes.en: And he must buy himself a path: the seller from the buyer, to walk through to his pit, for a seller sells generously and did not reserve a path for himself.

messages.text: He need not purchase a path, as the seller clearly did not intend to keep the pit or cistern without maintaining access to it.

notes.he: דמוכר בעין רעה מוכר ודרך שייר לו:
notes.en: He need not: for a seller sells grudgingly, and he reserved a path for himself.

notes.he: ליקח לו דרך דמוכר בעין רעה מוכר ושייר לעצמו דרך]:
notes.en: And the Rabbis say he need not buy himself a path, for a seller sells grudgingly and reserved a path for himself.

messages.text: And Rabbi Akiva concedes that when the seller states to the buyer in the document of sale: Excluding these, the pit and the cistern, that he need not purchase for himself a path through to the pit or cistern.

notes.dh: ומודה ר' עקיבא בזמן שאמר לו [מוכר ללוקח] כל הבית אני מוכר לך [חוץ מבור ודות
notes.he: זה שאינו צריך ליקח לו דרך] מה טעם הואיל ולא היה צריך לומר חוץ מזה ואמר לכך אמר לשייר לו דרך:
notes.en: And Rabbi Akiva concedes, when the seller said to the buyer, “I am selling you the whole house except the pit and the cistern,” that he need not buy himself a path. What is the reason? Since he did not need to say “except this,” and he said it, he said it in order to reserve a path for himself.

messages.text: Evidently, Rabbi Akiva’s reasoning is that since the seller need not specify that the pit and cistern are excluded from the sale, and yet he says that they were excluded, he is coming with this statement to add an element to the agreement, i.e., the right of access.

notes.he: מוכר ללוקח בית אני מוכר לך חוץ מאלו בור ודות שאין צריך ליקח לו דרך. אלמא כיון דלא צריך לפרושי דהא מסתמא נמי אין בור ודות בכלל הבית ופירש ודאי לטפויי מילתא קאמר ולהודיעו שמשייר לעצמו הכא נמי כיון דקומתי משמע נמי גובה קומתי וקאמר מלא אלמא לטפויי מילתא אתא ולהודיע שאין דעתו אלא למדת הגובה:
notes.en: When he said to him: the seller to the buyer: I am selling you a house except for these, the pit and the cistern; then he need not buy himself a path. Evidently, since he did not need to specify, for even without specifying the pit and cistern are not included in the house, and he specified, he certainly said it to add something, to let him know that he reserves [a path] for himself. Here too, since “my height” already implies the height of my stature, and he said “full,” evidently he came to add something, to let it be known that he intends only the measure of the height.

messages.text: Here too, when one says: It is incumbent upon me to donate my full height, since it is a case where he need not add the word full, and yet he says it, he is coming to add an element to his vow, i.e., the ability to exempt himself with a thin rod.

notes.he: כלומר הואיל ואינו צ"ל אלא קומתו עלי ואמר מלא קומתי לפחות קאמר:
notes.en: Here too: that is, since he needed to say only “my height is upon me,” and he said “my full height,” he meant something less.

notes.he: כלומר לכך הוסיף בדבורו. ואיכא דאמרי איפכא קומתי עלי נותן שרביט הנכפף מלא קומתי עלי נותן שרביט שאינו נכפף דכל לישנא (בתרא) [יתירא] לטפויי מלתא אתא:
notes.en: He is coming to add an element: that is, that is why he added to his words. And some say the reverse: “My height is upon me,” he gives a rod that bends; “my full height is upon me,” he gives a rod that does not bend, for all superfluous language comes to add an element.

messages.text: If one says: It is incumbent upon me to donate my stature, what is the halakha?
messages.lead: A dilemma was raised before the Sages:

notes.he: מי הוי משמע שרביט קומתו או לא:
notes.en: Omdi [my standing; the Davidson English renders “my stature”] is upon me: does it imply a rod of his height or not?

notes.he: יש לפרש כל הבעיות באם תמצא לומר והכי פי' עומדי מהו מי אמרינן שרוצה לומר שיתן שרביט שאינו נכפף או דלמא שרביט שיכול לעמוד בעינן ואע"פ שנכפף רחבי מהו אם תמצא לומר (דעמוד) [בעמדו נותן] שרביט [שנכפף] ברחבו מהו מי בעינן כרחבו ממש דרחבו אינו יכול לכפוף כשכופף קומתו אינו כופף רחבו הכי נמי משמע שרביט בלא כפיפה או דלמא רוצה לומר שרביט ארוך כרוחבו ואף על פי שנכפף ואת"ל ברוחבו נותן שרביט כפוף ישיבתי מהו מי אמרינן שר"ל בלא (הפיכה) [כפיפה] כלומר כמו שאני יושב מראשי ועד רגלי או דילמא שרביט כפוף משמע שהרי כשהוא יושב הוא כפוף ואם תמצא לומר דישיבתו משמע שרביט כפוף מפני שהוא כפוף ויושב עוביו מהו מי אמרינן ר"ל בלא כפיפה (בלא) [אלא] עב כעובי קומתו שהרי עוביו אינו כפוף או דילמא שרביט גדול כמלא עוביו קאמר ואף על פי שהוא כפוף ואם תמצא לומר דבעוביו משמע בכפיפה הקיפו מהו מי אמרינן שר"ל שרביט עד שמקיף כל גופו ועב כל כך שאינו יכול לחזור מכפיפתו או דילמא דבר שמקיפו קאמר ואפילו כל דהו ורבינו אלחנן פירש על ישיבתו מי אמרינן שר"ל מראשו ועד מקום ישיבתו קאמר שהוא חצי גופו או דילמא כל גופו קאמר כמו שהוא יושב מראשו ועד רגליו וי"מ ישיבתי מהו מי אמרינן שר"ל שיתן השרביט שיחזיק קומת ישיבתו ולא כמלא קומת עמידתו או דילמא שרביט שמחזיק מקום ישיבתו קאמר:
notes.en: In brief: All the dilemmas can be read as a chain of “if you say.” My standing: does he mean a rod that does not bend, or only a rod that can stand, even if it bends? If you say “my standing” lets him give a rod that bends, then my width: does he need a rod truly as wide as he is, which cannot be bent (when he bends his height he does not bend his width), or a rod as long as his width, even if it bends? If you say a rod that bends for width, then my sitting: does it mean without bending, as he sits from his head to his feet, or a bent rod, since a sitting person is bent? If you say sitting means a bent rod, then my thickness: is it a rod as thick as his body, unbent, since his thickness does not bend, or a large rod the full measure of his thickness even if it bends? If you say thickness allows bending, then my girth: a rod that goes around his whole body and is so thick it cannot be unbent, or anything that goes around him, however thin? Rabbeinu Elḥanan explained “my sitting” as either from his head to the place where he sits, half his body, or his whole body as he sits, head to feet; and some explain it as a rod that matches his sitting height rather than his standing height, or a rod that holds the place where he sits. Open on Sefaria for the full text.

notes.he: אמר עומדי עלי [מהו] יש בלשון הזה לשון נדרים או לא:
notes.en: Omdi, what is the halakha?: if he said “omdi is upon me,” what is the halakha: is this wording the language of vows or not?

messages.text: If one vowed that it is incumbent upon him to donate his width, what is the halakha? Likewise, if one vowed to donate his sitting, what is the halakha? If he referred to his thickness, what is the halakha? Finally, if he spoke of his girth, what is the halakha?

notes.he: עלי מהו מי הוי משמע שרביט רוחב דוגמתי או הוי משמע שרביט ארוך כמדת רחבי:
notes.en: My width is upon me, what is the halakha? Does it imply a rod as wide as I am, or does it imply a long rod the measure of my width?

notes.he: מי יהיב שרביט נכפף וארוך כמדת היקפו או דילמא שרביט עב כהקיפו בעי למיתב. תיקו:
notes.en: My girth, what is the halakha? Does he give a rod that bends, as long as the measure of his girth, or perhaps he must give a rod as thick as his girth? Let it stand.

messages.text: These dilemmas shall stand unresolved.

messages.caption: Vowing one’s height: the rod Rav Yehuda and the baraita require, and the five dilemmas left standing.

messages.text: The mishna teaches that there is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei concerning one who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate the weight of my forearm, as to how he ascertains the weight of his forearm. The Sages taught this dispute in greater detail in a baraita:
messages.quote: the weight of my forearm, how does he ascertain the weight of his forearm

messages.text: With regard to one who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate the weight of my forearm, and with regard to one who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate the weight of my leg,
He brings a barrel and fills it with water, and he inserts his forearm up to the elbow or his leg up to the knee, into the water.

notes.he: מרפק:
notes.en: Atzil: the elbow [marpek].

notes.he: ומכאן ולמעלה לא הוי רגל אלא ירך:
notes.en: Up to the knee: and from there upward it is not “leg” but thigh.

notes.he: היינו מרפיקו]:
notes.en: Up to the atzil: that is, his marpek.

messages.text: And in order to measure the displacement, he weighs donkey flesh, sinews, and bones, and places it into the barrel until it fills, and the water reaches the same level as it was when his arm or leg was inserted. And even though there is no proof for the matter, that donkey flesh weighs the same as human flesh, nevertheless there is an allusion to the matter, as it is stated: “Whose flesh is as the flesh of donkeys.”

verse.he: וַתַּעְגְּבָה עַל פִּלַגְשֵׁיהֶם אֲשֶׁר בְּשַׂר־חֲמוֹרִים בְּשָׂרָם וְזִרְמַת סוּסִים זִרְמָתָם׃
verse.en: she lusted for concubinage with them, whose members were like those of donkeys and whose organs were like those of stallions.

notes.dh: ושוקל בשר חמור גידים ועצמות ונותן לתוכה עד שתתמלא
notes.he: ותימה לר' אלחנן כיון דשקל כבר בשר חמור כנגד משקל ידו אמאי נותן עוד בשר חמור בחבית והיה נראה לו דה"פ דשוקל בשר גידין חמור כשנתן בשר לתוך המים עד שתתמלא ונותן קודם לתוך המים הבשר עד שתתמלא החבית ואח"כ שוקל כנגד ידו ואני מצאתי בשם ר"י דוקא נקט שוקל מעיקרא ואח"כ מכניס אבל מכניס מעיקרא לא לפי שהמים נבלעים בבשר ומכבידים אותו יותר מדאי מיד האדם שחי נושא עצמו וחייא קליל ממיתא ודוחק הוא לומר ששוקלין בשר חמור כנגד היד אם הוא נחתך ששוקל יותר משהיה מחובר לגוף לגמרי:
notes.en: And he weighs donkey flesh, sinews and bones, and places it into it until it fills: Rabbeinu Elḥanan found this puzzling: since he has already weighed donkey flesh against the weight of his arm, why does he put still more donkey flesh into the barrel? It seemed to him that this is the meaning: he weighs the donkey flesh and sinews once he has put the flesh into the water until it filled; that is, first he puts the flesh into the water until the barrel fills, and afterward he weighs it as the measure of his arm. But I found in the name of Ri that it says “weighs” first deliberately, and afterward he puts it in; not putting it in first, because the water is absorbed into the flesh and makes it heavier than the person’s arm, for a living person carries himself, and the living is lighter than the dead. And it is a stretch to say that they weigh donkey flesh against the arm as it would be if cut off, for it would then weigh more than when it was wholly attached to the body.

notes.he: שנמשל בשר חמור לבשר אדם [לפיכך אומדין בבשר חמור]:
notes.en: An allusion to the matter: that donkey flesh is compared to human flesh; therefore they estimate with donkey flesh.

messages.text: @Rabbi Yehuda Displacement is according to volume, not according to weight, and how then is it possible to match the amount of the donkey flesh with the flesh in one’s forearm, the sinews with the sinews, and the bones with the bones?
@Rabbi Yosei One estimates.
@Rabbi Yehuda If one estimates, let one estimate the weight of the forearm directly.
And how does Rabbi Yehuda respond to Rabbi Yosei? Rabbi Yehuda holds that we do whatever is possible in order to be more precise.

notes.he: לשעורי במים ובאומד משערינן:
notes.en: As far as possible: we measure with the water, and what we cannot, we measure by estimate.

messages.text: The Tosefta teaches with regard to one who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate the weight of my forearm [yad], that Rabbi Yehuda says: He brings a barrel and fills it with water and inserts his forearm up to the elbow. This indicates that the term yad denotes the forearm until the elbow.
messages.quote: inserts his forearm up to the elbow

notes.he: למימרא דעד העציל קרי [יד]:
notes.en: And the arm up to the atzil: that is to say, up to the atzil is called yad.

messages.text: Since it is written: “And Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands [yedeihem] and their feet,” the priests are obligated to sanctify their hands and feet in the Temple up to the wrist.
messages.lead: And the Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita:

verse.he: וְרָחֲצוּ אַהֲרֹן וּבָנָיו מִמֶּנּוּ אֶת־יְדֵיהֶם וְאֶת־רַגְלֵיהֶם׃
verse.en: and let Aaron and his sons wash their hands and feet [in water drawn] from it.

notes.he: מקום חיבור הכף והזרוע. אלמא יד לא הוי אלא עד הפרק דהא יד כתיב בקרא:
notes.en: Up to the joint: the place where the palm and the arm join. Evidently yad is only up to the joint, since yad is written in the verse.

notes.he: [עד מקום] שכלה פיסת יד:
notes.en: Up to the joint: up to the place where the palm of the hand ends.

messages.text: The term yad written in the Torah indicates up to the wrist, but with regard to vows one follows the ordinary language of people, in which the word yad is referring to the forearm until the elbow. Consequently, the vow is interpreted in this manner.

notes.dh: בנדרים הלך אחר לשון בני אדם
notes.he: ועד העציל קורין בני אדם יד:
notes.en: With regard to vows, follow the language of people: and people call it yad up to the atzil.

messages.text: And does the word yad that is written in the Torah mean up to the wrist? But with regard to phylacteries it is written: “And it shall be for a sign to you upon your hand [yadkha],”

verse.he: וְהָיָה לְךָ לְאוֹת עַל־יָדְךָ וּלְזִכָּרוֹן בֵּין עֵינֶיךָ לְמַעַן תִּהְיֶה תּוֹרַת יְהֹוָה בְּפִיךָ כִּי בְּיָד חֲזָקָה הוֹצִאֲךָ יְהֹוָה מִמִּצְרָיִם׃
verse.en: “And this shall serve you as a sign on your hand and as a reminder on your forehead—in order that GOD’s Teaching may be in your mouth—that with a mighty hand GOD freed you from Egypt.

messages.text: Yadkha; this is referring to the bulge of the biceps [kibborit] on the upper arm.

notes.he: שקורין שוריץ אלמא דעד התם קרוי יד מדאורייתא:
notes.en: This is the kibborit: which is called (a vernacular gloss). Evidently up to there it is called yad by Torah law.

messages.text: Generally, the term yad that is written in the Torah includes the entire biceps area of the upper arm. But with regard to vows one follows the ordinary language of people, in which the word yad means the forearm until the elbow; and with regard to sanctifying the hands and feet in the Temple the halakha is learned as a tradition that the word yad is referring only to the hand up to the wrist.

notes.he: קרוי יד עד האציל:
notes.en: The language of people: it is called yad up to the atzil.

notes.he: ברדו"ן בלע"ז בגובה הזרוע רחוק מן האציל מעט:
notes.en: Kibbora: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), at the top of the arm, a little distance from the atzil.

notes.dh: בנדרים הלך אחר לשון בני אדם
notes.he: ועד העציל קורין יד היינו למעלה מקיבורת:
notes.en: With regard to vows, follow the language of people: and people call it yad up to the atzil, that is, above the kibborit.

notes.he: ועד הפרק הלכתא גמירי לה:
notes.en: [The editor notes: it seems the text should read, “and that the sanctification of hands and feet is up to the joint is a halakha,” and so on.] And “up to the joint” they learned as a halakha [by tradition].

messages.text: It is further taught in the Tosefta cited above: His leg [regel] until the knee, which indicates that the term regel is defined as the foot until the knee.
messages.quote: his leg up to the knee

notes.he: יינויל בלע"ז]:
notes.en: Rekhuba [the knee]: (an Old French gloss).

messages.text: It is written in the Torah with regard to the obligation to ascend to Jerusalem for the pilgrimage Festivals: “Three times [regalim] you shall keep a feast for Me in the year.” The term regalim, legs, serves to exclude people with artificial legs [ba’alei kabbayin] from this obligation.
messages.lead: And the Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita:

verse.en: Three times a year you shall hold a festival for Me:

notes.he: שלש רגלים בשנה:
notes.en: Regalim: three pilgrimage Festivals a year.

notes.he: מי שנחתך רגלו בפרק ראשון סמוך לשוקו וחוקק קב מקבל כתיתין ונותן שוקו לתוכה וקורין אשקנצ"א שפטור מן הראיה דאין לו רגל. אלמא לא מיקרי רגל אלא עד פרק א' שקורין קביל"א:
notes.en: Excluding those with artificial legs [ba’alei kabbin]: one whose foot was cut off at the first joint near his shin, and he hollows out a kav lined with rags and puts his shin into it, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). He is exempt from the appearance [at the Temple], since he has no regel. Evidently it is called regel only up to the first joint, which is called (an Old French gloss).

notes.he: הקשה רבינו אלחנן היכי משמע מהכא דרגל קרי עד האיסתוירא ודילמא היינו טעמא שאינו יכול לישען עליו ואפי' קרית נמי רגל עד הארכובה וכי קא ממעטינן נמי בחגיגה פ"ק (דף ג. ושם) חיגר וסומא מפני שאינו יכול לילך ולישען בלי מקל ותירץ דהתם בחגיגה איכא שני דרשות מרגלים דחדא דריש חיגר וסומא מטעם שאינן יכולין לילך ולישען בלא שום דבר אע"פ שיש להם רגל ובחדא דריש רגלים פרט לבעלי קבין מטעם שאין לו רגל:
notes.en: Regalim excludes those with artificial legs: Rabbeinu Elḥanan asked: how is it implied from here that regel means only up to the ankle [istaveira]? Perhaps the reason is that he cannot lean on it, even if you call it regel up to the knee; for indeed in the first chapter of Ḥagiga (3a) we also exclude the lame and the blind, because they cannot walk and lean without a staff. And he answered that there in Ḥagiga there are two expositions of “regalim”: from one it excludes the lame and the blind, for the reason that they cannot walk and lean without something, even though they have a leg; and from the other it expounds “regalim, excluding those with artificial legs,” for the reason that he has no leg.

messages.text: According to the baraita, one who has a stump in place of his foot is exempt from the pilgrimage. This indicates the term regel is referring to the foot, up to the ankle, not to the entire area below the knee.

notes.he: מה שכתוב שלש רגלים לומר שמי שיש לו רגלים יעלה לרגל פרט למי שיש לו רגל של עץ והיינו קבין שחוקק כעין קב ומניח שוקו בו ואמאי פטור הא עדיין נשאר לו רגל עד הארכובה דעד התם קרי [אינשי] רגל:
notes.en: Regalim excludes those with artificial legs: what is written, “three regalim,” is to say that one who has legs shall go up for the Festival, excluding one who has a leg of wood, that is, kabbin: one hollows out something like a kav and puts his shin into it. But why is he exempt? He still has a leg up to the knee! [The editor notes that here one should mark the answer: “With regard to vows, follow the language of people,”] for up to there people call it regel.

messages.text: The term regel that is written in the Torah is referring to the foot below the ankle, but with regard to vows, one follows the ordinary language of people, in which the word regel means the leg until the knee.
And does regel written in the Torah mean the foot up to the ankle, and therefore it serves to exclude people with artificial legs?

But with regard to the ritual by which the yavam frees the yevama of her levirate bonds [ḥalitza], it is written: “Then his brother’s wife shall approach…and loose his shoe from upon his foot [raglo],”

verse.he: וְנִגְּשָׁה יְבִמְתּוֹ אֵלָיו לְעֵינֵי הַזְּקֵנִים וְחָלְצָה נַעֲלוֹ מֵעַל רַגְלוֹ וְיָרְקָה בְּפָנָיו וְעָנְתָה וְאָמְרָה כָּכָה יֵעָשֶׂה לָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יִבְנֶה אֶת־בֵּית אָחִיו׃
verse.en: his brother’s widow shall go up to him in the presence of the elders, pull the sandal off his foot, spit in his face, and make this declaration: Thus shall be done to the man who will not build up his brother’s house!

messages.text: In the case of a yavam who was missing part of his leg, if the yevama performed the ḥalitza on any part of the leg from the knee and below, her ḥalitza is valid.
messages.lead: and the Sages taught in a mishna:

notes.he: למי שנחתך רגל ונשתייר בו קצת מן הארכובה ולמטה חליצתה כשירה. אלמא עד הארכובה הוי רגל וליחייב בראיה:
notes.en: She performed ḥalitza: on one whose leg was cut off and a little of it remained from the knee downward, her ḥalitza is valid. Evidently up to the knee is regel, so let him be obligated in the appearance [at the Temple].

notes.he: שנחתכה הרגל ונשתייר מעט מן הארכובה ולמטה חליצתה כשירה ל' רש"י. ולא נהירא שהרי ביבמות (דף קג. ושם) אמר דאפי' חלצה למי שנהפכה רגלו חליצתה פסולה לכך צריך לפרש דמיירי הכא מקשרי הרצועות של המנעל שאם קשרן מהארכובה ולמטה כשרה דהוי שפיר וחלצה נעלו מעל רגלו אבל אם קשרן למעלה חליצתו פסולה דאין זה מעל רגלו:
notes.en: She performed ḥalitza: where the leg was cut off and a little remained from the knee downward, her ḥalitza is valid; so Rashi. This does not seem right, for in Yevamot (103a) it says that even if she performed ḥalitza for one whose foot was turned backward, her ḥalitza is invalid. Therefore one must explain that it speaks here of where the straps of the shoe are tied: if they were tied from the knee downward it is valid, since this is properly “she removed his shoe from upon his foot”; but if they were tied above, his ḥalitza is invalid, for this is not “from upon his foot.”

messages.text: This indicates that the term regel in the Torah means the leg from the foot up to the knee.

notes.he: [מן הארכובה חליצתה כשרה אלמא דעד הארכובה איקרי רגל מן התורה]:
notes.en: From the knee and below her ḥalitza is valid: evidently up to the knee is called regel by Torah law.

messages.text: The term regel in the Torah actually is referring to the foot, below the ankle, and it is different there, with regard to ḥalitza, as the verse states: From upon his foot [raglo], instead of simply stating: From his foot. This indicates that the area that is upon, i.e., above, the foot is also valid for the performance of ḥalitza.

notes.he: משמע מה שעל רגלו דהיינו שוק עד הארכובה:
notes.en: From upon his foot: implies what is upon his foot, that is, the shin, up to the knee.

notes.he: של מעלה מרגלו יכולה לחלוץ:
notes.en: From upon his foot: she may perform ḥalitza on what is above his foot.

messages.text: If that is so, then if the yevama performed ḥalitza above the knee it should also be valid.
It is written: From upon, to include only the section directly above the foot, i.e., until the knee, and the area above the knee is considered from upon that area that is from upon the foot.

Conclude from this discussion that the ankle bone [istaveira] descends to the ground and is not separated from the foot. The reason is that if it enters your mind to say it is separated, then the ankle bone is the section of the leg referred to by the phrase: From upon his foot, and the lower leg, i.e., the section of the leg from the ankle up to the knee, is the section of the leg that is called: From upon that which is from upon the foot, and would therefore be invalid for the performance of ḥalitza.

notes.he: מדלא חשיב שוק עד הארכובה מעל דמעל:
notes.en: Conclude from it: since it does not count the shin, up to the knee, as “from upon that which is from upon.”

notes.he: קביל"א עד ארעא נחית שאין בה אלא פרק עליון המחברה עם השוק אבל למטה אין בה פרק אלא מעצם כף הרגל הוא דאי ס"ד למטה נמי פסיק הוה ליה איסתוירא כו':
notes.en: This istaveira, (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), descends to the ground: for it has only an upper joint, connecting it to the shin, but below it has no joint; rather, it is of a piece with the bone of the sole of the foot. For if it entered your mind that below it too is separate, the istaveira would be, and so on.

notes.he: שקורין קאבילא]:
notes.en: Istaveira: which is called (an Old French gloss).

notes.he: ואין בו פיסוק עד סוף העקב:
notes.en: Descends to the ground: and it has no separation down to the end of the heel.

notes.he: שוק הוא עצם שמגיע עד הארכובה:
notes.en: And the shin is “from upon that which is from upon”: the shin is the bone that reaches up to the knee.

messages.text: Even if you say the ankle is separated from the foot it would still not be referred to as the section that is upon the foot, as anything that is adjacent to the foot is considered like the foot, i.e., it is part of the same section of the leg as the foot.

messages.caption: How far yad and regel reach: in vows, in the Torah, and in the Temple, the Festivals and ḥalitza.

messages.text: Mishna

If one vows: It is incumbent upon me to donate the assessment of my forearm, the court appraises him to determine how much he is worth with a forearm and how much he is worth without a forearm, and he pays the difference.

This is a halakha that is more stringent with regard to vows of assessment than with regard to valuations, as one who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate the valuation of my forearm, is exempt from paying.

notes.he: דאילו אמר בערכין ערך ידי עלי ערך רגלי עלי לא אמר כלום אלא א"כ אמר בדבר שהנשמה תלויה בה:
notes.en: Mishna. This is a stringency of vows over valuations: for in valuations, if he said “the valuation of my hand is upon me” or “the valuation of my foot is upon me,” he has said nothing, unless he said it of something on which life depends.

notes.he: שבערכין אם אמר ערך ידי עלי לא אמר כלום:
notes.en: This is a stringency of vows over valuations: for in valuations, if he said “the valuation of my hand is upon me,” he has said nothing.

notes.he: שהערך הוא קצוב בתורה]:
notes.en: The heirs shall give: for the valuation is fixed in the Torah. [This glosses the mishna’s next line, “a stringency of valuations over vows,” which appears at the top of 20a.]

messages.text: Gemara
How do we assess him?
messages.quote: the court appraises him to determine how much he is worth with a forearm and how much he is worth without a forearm

messages.text: The court assesses him by means of the same process of assessment used with regard to the halakhot of damages. If one’s hand was severed, the court considers the injured party as though he is a slave being sold in the slave market and appraises how much he was worth before the injury and how much he is worth after the injury. The difference between these two sums is the amount that the guilty party must pay for damages.

notes.he: כמו שאומדין אדם שקיטע לו חבירו ידו שמין אותו כעבד הנמכר בשוק כמה היה יפה קודם לכן וכמה הוא יפה עכשיו:
notes.en: Gemara. The assessment of damages: as one assesses a person whose hand his fellow cut off: they appraise him like a slave being sold in the market, how much he was worth before and how much he is worth now.

notes.he: [שאומדים כמה רוצה אדם ליתן יותר בעבד שיש לו יד יותר מעבד שאין לו אלא יד אחת כמו שאומדים בנזיקין]. כדתנן נזק כיצד קיטע את ידו רואים אותו כאילו הוא [עבד] נמכר כמה היה יפה וכמה הוא יפה:
notes.en: The assessment of damages: they estimate how much more a person is willing to give for a slave who has another hand than for a slave who has only one hand, as they assess in damages; as we learned: Damage, how so? If he cut off his hand, they view him as though he were a slave being sold, how much he was worth and how much he is worth.

messages.text: @Rava Are these two assessments comparable? There, with regard to damages, the person has depreciated in value because his hand was severed, and therefore the decline in the assessment is greater for someone with a severed hand than for someone who merely lacks the utility of his hand. Here, with regard to one who vowed to donate the assessment of his forearm, the person himself has good value, as his hand is intact, and if the assessment used with regard to damages is applied to him he would be obligated to pay more than that which he vowed.
messages.quote: the same process of assessment used with regard to the halakhot of damages

notes.he: שכבר נקטעה ידו ואפי' תחילת דמיו שאומדין עתה כמה היה יפה קודם לכן אין נישומין אלא בזול שהרי רואין אותו מזולזל:
notes.en: There the man is depreciated: for his hand has already been cut off, and even his original value, when they now estimate how much he was worth before, is appraised only cheaply, for they see him as depreciated.

notes.he: ששתי ידיו שלימות וצריך לשום כמה הוא יפה עכשיו שיקדיש דמיו וכמה הוא יפה אם יחתכו ידיו:
notes.en: Here the man is of good value: for both his hands are whole, and one must appraise how much he is worth now, since he consecrates his value, and how much he would be worth if his hands were cut off.

notes.he: פירש"י שכבר נקטעה ידו ואפי' תחילת דמיו שאומדין [עתה כמה היה יפה] קודם לכן אין שמין אלא בזול שהרי רואין אותו מזולזל וקשה לר"י על פירוש זה מאי שנא מנודר הא רחמנא אמר בנודר (שמות כ״א:ל׳) ונתן פדיון נפשו שיש לו ליתן כל דמיו ה"נ גבי נזיקין שאמר הכתוב לשום כל דמיו משלם ועוד קשה מאי היא דאמר לקמן ואידך פסיקא היינו הך פי' ששמין יד העבד כמי שאין לו אלא יד אחת והאחרת נפסקת היינו הך דאומד של נזיקין אדרבה לאו היינו של נזיקין דהא נזיקין שיימינן פחות מכדי שויו של חיים שהרי כשנקטעה ידו הוא נמאס אבל הכא גבי עבד אע"ג דידו אחת נפסקה מ"מ אמלאכת ידו אחת אנו שמין משלם וגברא שביח הוא ונראה לר"י דהכי פי' אמר לו אביי מי דמי התם גברא זילא הוא גבי נזקין שהרי כשנקטעה ידו הוא נמאס יותר משהיה לו יד ונקשר ולפיכך יש לו לשום לפי הזלזול אבל הכא גבי נודר גברא שביח הוא שהרי שתי ידיו שלימות הילכך שמין אותו פחות משוייו ושמין אותו כמו שהיתה ידו מוכתב למלכות (אחר):
notes.en: There the man is depreciated: Rashi explained: his hand has already been cut off, and even his original value is appraised only cheaply, since they see him as depreciated. Ri objects to this explanation. First, how is this different from one who vows? The Torah says of the one who vows (Exodus 21:30), “he shall give the redemption of his life,” that he must give his full value; so too with damages, where the verse says to assess his full value, he pays. Second, what is meant below by “and the other is severed; that is the same thing,” namely that they assess the slave’s hand as one who has only one hand and the other cut off, and that this is the same as the assessment of damages? On the contrary, that is not the assessment of damages, for in damages we assess at less than his worth as a whole person, since once his hand was cut off he is repulsive; but here, with the slave, even though one hand is cut off, we still assess by the work of his one hand in full, and he is a man of good value. So Ri explains: Abaye said, is it comparable? There, in damages, the man is depreciated, for once his hand was cut off he is more repulsive than had he a hand that was merely bound, so he must be assessed according to the depreciation; but here, with the one who vows, the man is of good value, for both his hands are whole; therefore they assess him at less than his worth, assessing him as though his hand were written over to the government.

notes.he: בנזיקין:
notes.en: There: in damages.

notes.he: שקטועה ידו הילכך שיימינן ליה [בגברא] זילא ששמין אותו בעבד קטוע שכיון שקטוע הוא מזולזל הוא ופוחתין דמיו:
notes.en: A depreciated man: whose hand is cut off; therefore we assess him as a depreciated man, assessing him as a maimed slave, for since he is maimed he is depreciated and his value is lowered.

notes.he: באומר דמי ידי [עלי]:
notes.en: Here: one who says “the value of my hand is upon me.”

notes.he: אדם שלם הוא שאם ישומו אותו [עכשיו] כמה הוא שוה שלם וכמה הוא שוה קטוע יעלו דמיו הרבה עכשיו כשעדיין הוא שלם אבל אם ישומו אותו כאדם קיטוע שהוא מזולזל כמה הוא שוה עכשיו וכמה הוא שוה קודם לכן יפחתו דמיו של זה יותר ממה שאם ישומו אותו בעצמו שהוא שלם ונמצא הקדש מפסיד:
notes.en: He is a man of good value: he is a whole person. If they assess him now, how much he is worth whole and how much he is worth maimed, his value comes out high, now that he is still whole. But if they assess him like a maimed man, who is depreciated, how much he is worth now and how much before, his value would be lowered more than if they assess him as himself, whole, and the Temple treasury would lose.

messages.text: One assesses how much less a person is willing to pay for a slave who works with one hand than for a slave who works with two hands.

notes.he: אותו כאיש שלם כמה אדם רוצה כו':
notes.en: Rather, Abaye said: one assesses him as a whole man, how much a person is willing, and so on.

messages.text: What is the case of a slave who works with one hand? Isn’t this a situation where the other hand is severed? If so, then this assessment is identical to that which Rava proposed.

notes.dh: ידו אחת מאי ניהו ואידך פסיקא
notes.he: כלומר למה הוא עושה מלאכה בידו אחת שהאחרת קטועה היינו אומד של נזקין:
notes.en: His one hand, what is it, and the other is severed?: that is, why does he work with one hand? Because the other is cut off; that is the assessment of damages.

notes.dh: עושה מלאכה בידו אחת מאי ניהו אילימא דאידך [ידו] פסוקה
notes.he: קטועה היינו הך דאמרי ברישא אומד של נזיקין:
notes.en: Who works with one hand, what is that? If you say his other hand is severed, cut off, that is the same as what was said at first, the assessment of damages.

messages.text: Rather, one assesses how much more a person is willing to pay for a slave who belongs exclusively to him than for a case where it is written in his bill of sale that his first owner reserves ownership of one hand of the slave.

notes.he: שלא יעשה בה מלאכה לרבו שני דהשתא שיימינן כגברא שביחא:
notes.en: His hand is written over to his first master: so that he may not do work with it for his second master; for now we appraise him as a man of good value.

notes.he: שמשמכרו רבו ראשון שייר לעצמו ידו אחת שיעשה מלאכת רבו בה ועבד שלם הוא:
notes.en: Rather, the other hand is written over to his first master: when his first master sold him, he reserved one of his hands for himself, that he do his master’s work with it; and he is a whole slave.

messages.text: The mishna in Sanhedrin 2a states that the valuation of a person for the purpose of a vow must be performed by nine judges and one priest. By contrast, the valuation of someone for the purpose of damages is performed by three judges. With this in mind:

If one was damaged by another and the court assesses him by the assessment of damages, i.e., with three judges, and then he says: My assessment is incumbent upon me, what is the halakha? Does one say that as his assessment was already assessed one time for damages, this is the amount he must donate? Or perhaps an assessment performed by ten is different from an assessment performed by three, and therefore it is necessary to repeat the assessment with ten judges.

notes.he: שחבל בו חבירו ואמדוהו כמה היה יפה וכמה הוא יפה:
notes.en: They assessed him by the assessment of damages: his fellow injured him, and they assessed how much he was worth and how much he is worth.

notes.he: ולא אמר ערכי עלי מיבעי תו למישיימיה או לא:
notes.en: And he said “my assessment is upon me”: and he did not say “my valuation is upon me.” Must he be appraised again or not?

notes.he: שהאומר דמי עלי נישום בעשרה כדתנן פ"ק דסנהדרין (דף ב.) הקרקעות תשעה וכהן ואדם כיוצא בהן ואומד של נזקין בשלשה כדתנן גזילות וחבלות בשלשה:
notes.en: An assessment by ten: for one who says “my assessment is upon me” is appraised by ten, as we learned in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (2a): land, by nine and a priest, and a person likewise; and the assessment of damages is by three, as we learned: robbery and injuries, by three.

notes.dh: או דילמא שאני אומד דבי עשרה
notes.he: כדתניא בפ"ק דסנהדרין (דף טו. ושם) הקרקעות כו' וכהן ואדם כיוצא בהן משום דעשרה כהנים כתיבי בפרשה כדפירש"י והקשה רבינו אלחנן אמאי אין צריך יותר מעשרה והא בית דין שקול הוא וכל מלתא דתלויה בסברא צריך הכרע והכי נמי קרי ליה בית דין ואין ב"ד שקול מוסיפין עליהן עוד אחד ויהא י"א שבכל בתי דינין של ממון ודיני נפשות אמר אין ב"ד שקול מוסיפין עליהן עוד אחד בפ"ק דסנהדרין (דף ב:) [וע"ע תוס' מגילה כ"ג: ד"ה עשרה]:
notes.en: Or perhaps an assessment by ten is different: as it is taught in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (15a): land [is assessed by nine and a priest], and a person likewise, because ten mentions of “priest” are written in the passage, as Rashi explained. And Rabbeinu Elḥanan asked: why are no more than ten needed? Is this not an evenly balanced court, and any matter that depends on judgment needs a deciding voice? And it is also called a court, and a court is not made even: one more is added to it, making eleven; for of all courts, in monetary and capital cases, it says “a court is not made even; one more is added to them,” in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (2b). [And see further Tosafot on Megilla 23b, s.v. asara.]

notes.he: כגון שהוזק ושמוהו:
notes.en: They assessed him by the assessment of damages: for example, he was injured and they assessed him.

notes.he: מי צריך לאומדו עוד או אינו צריך:
notes.en: And he said “my assessment is upon me,” what is the halakha? Must he be assessed again, or need he not?

notes.he: דבערכין צריך עשרה בני אדם לאומדו דעשרה כהנים כתובים בפרשה ואומד של נזקין בג' בתי דינין סגיא:
notes.en: An assessment by ten is different: for in valuations ten people are needed to assess him, since ten mentions of “priest” are written in the passage, while for the assessment of damages a court of three suffices.

messages.text: If you say an assessment performed by ten is different from an assessment performed by three, then in a case where one says: My assessment is incumbent upon me, and the court assessed him, and then he again says: My assessment is incumbent upon me, what is the halakha? Does one say that here he was certainly assessed by ten and there is no need for another assessment, or perhaps there is a concern that in the interim there might have been an enhancement in his assessment?

notes.he: [שוב] משנאמד בראשונה וצריך לשומו עוד:
notes.en: Or perhaps he increased in value in the interim: after he was first assessed, and he must be assessed again.

messages.text: Furthermore, if you say in that case there is a concern that in the interim his assessment might have increased and it is therefore necessary to assess him a second time, then with regard to one who says: My assessment is incumbent upon me, and the court did not yet assess him, and then before the court assesses him he again says: My assessment is incumbent upon me, what is the halakha? Do we say that here certainly …

Continues on 20a: … we assess him once and he gives twice that sum, or, since he vowed one after the other, we assess him twice? Rava goes on to ask about one who says at once: “My assessment is twice upon me.”
